details:
**Partitions of Poland**
Three partitions in 1772, 1793, and 1795, in which Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided up the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth until it vanished from the map. The first came after the Bar Confederation's failed revolt, Catherine the Great's Russia was the leading power behind them, and Poland did not regain independence until 1918.

**Sejm and the liberum veto**
The Sejm is the Polish parliament. Under the old Commonwealth, the liberum veto let any single deputy cancel a session and all of its legislation, which paralyzed the government and let foreign powers bribe deputies to block reform.

**Constitution of May 3, 1791**
A reform constitution passed by the Great Sejm under King Stanisław II August that abolished the liberum veto. Conservative nobles formed the Targowica Confederation and asked Russia to overturn it, which led to the Second Partition.

**Invasion of Poland (September 1, 1939)**
Nazi Germany's invasion that started World War II in Europe, followed by a Soviet invasion from the east on September 17. It was justified by the Gleiwitz incident, a staged attack on a German radio station by SS men in Polish uniforms (Operation Canned Goods), and the invasion was followed by the Western "Phoney War."

**Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact**
The August 1939 non-aggression pact between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, whose secret protocol split Poland between them. Germany invaded nine days after it was signed.

**Solidarity and Lech Wałęsa**
Solidarity was the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc, founded in 1980 at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk and led by electrician Lech Wałęsa. Banned under General Wojciech Jaruzelski's 1981 martial law, it negotiated the 1989 Round Table Talks, won the following election using posters of Gary Cooper from High Noon, and Wałęsa became president.

**Union of Lublin and Jogaila-Jadwiga marriage**
The 1386 marriage of Queen Jadwiga of Poland to Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania created a personal union and the Jagiellonian dynasty. The 1569 Union of Lublin, under the last Jagiellonian king Sigismund II Augustus, turned it into the single Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

**Golden Liberty and the szlachta**
The szlachta were Poland's very large noble class, about a tenth of the population, who claimed descent from the ancient Sarmatians. Their "Golden Liberty" system, based on laws like Nihil Novi (1505), gave them an elective monarchy, the liberum veto, and the right to legal revolt (rokosz).

**Henrician Articles**
Terms that every elected Polish king had to swear to, named for Henry of Valois (later Henry III of France), the first king chosen by free election in 1573. Each king also signed a personal agreement called the pacta conventa.

**The Deluge**
The devastating mid-1600s Swedish invasion under Charles X Gustav during the Second Northern War, which came after the Khmelnytsky Uprising of the Cossacks. It killed around a third of Poland's population and cost the Commonwealth Livonia.

**John III Sobieski and the Winged Hussars**
King John III Sobieski led the relief army, spearheaded by Poland's famous Winged Hussars (heavy cavalry who wore wings on their backs), that broke the Ottoman Siege of Vienna in 1683. Legend says the first bagel was made to honor him.

**Warsaw Ghetto Uprising and Nazi camps**
In 1943, Jewish fighters of the ŻOB revolted in the Warsaw Ghetto, the largest Jewish ghetto in occupied Europe, until SS general Jürgen Stroop crushed them and deported the survivors to Treblinka. Major Nazi death camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau stood in occupied Poland, and the separate 1944 Warsaw Uprising saw the Wola massacre.

**Piast dynasty**
Poland's first ruling dynasty, which included Bolesław the Brave and Casimir the Great. Henry the Pious, a Piast duke, died fighting the Mongols at the 1241 Battle of Legnica; the Jagiellonians came after the Piasts.

**Tadeusz Kościuszko**
A Polish military engineer who helped the Americans win the Battle of Saratoga in the Revolutionary War. He led the 1794 Kościuszko Uprising against Russia, whose defeat (including the Massacre of Praga) led to the Third Partition.

**Battle of Klushino and Augustus the Strong**
At Klushino in 1610, Polish forces crushed a Russian-Swedish army during the Time of Troubles and went on to occupy Moscow until Minin and Pozharsky drove them out. Later, Augustus the Strong, Elector of Saxony, became Catholic to win the Polish throne and fought Sweden alongside Peter the Great in the Great Northern War.
